Ron Rivest :: Research :: Algorithms :: chunk_0003
In 1973, Rivest and his coauthors published the first [selection algorithm](/wiki/Selection_algorithm "Selection algorithm") that achieved [linear time](/wiki/Linear_time "Linear time") without using [randomization](/wiki/Randomization "Randomization").[[A1]](#CITEREFA1)[[12]](#cite_note-12) Their algorithm, the [median of medians](/wiki/Median_of_medians "Median of medians") method, is commonly taught in algorithms courses.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Rivest is also one of the two namesakes of the [Floyd–Rivest algorithm](/wiki/Floyd%E2%80%93Rivest_algorithm "Floyd–Rivest algorithm"), a randomized selection algorithm that achieves a near-optimal number of comparisons.[[A2]](#CITEREFA2)[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Rivest's 1974 doctoral dissertation concerned the use of [hash tables](/wiki/Hash_table "Hash table") to quickly match [partial words](/wiki/Partial_word "Partial word") in documents; he later published this work as a journal paper.[[A3]](#CITEREFA3) His research from this time on [self-organizing lists](/wiki/Self-organizing_list "Self-organizing list")[[A4]](#CITEREFA4) became one of the important precursors to the development of [competitive analysis](/wiki/Competitive_analysis_(online_algorithm) "Competitive analysis (online algorithm)") for [online algorithms](/wiki/Online_algorithm "Online algorithm").[[15]](#cite_note-15) In the early 1980s, he also published well-cited research on two-dimensional [bin packing problems](/wiki/Bin_packing_problem "Bin packing problem"),[[A5]](#CITEREFA5) and on [channel routing](/wiki/Channel_routing "Channel routing") in [VLSI design](/wiki/VLSI_design "VLSI design").[[A6]](#CITEREFA6)

He is a co-author of *[Introduction to Algorithms](/wiki/Introduction_to_Algorithms "Introduction to Algorithms")* (also known as *CLRS*), a standard textbook on algorithms, with [Thomas H. Cormen](/wiki/Thomas_H._Cormen "Thomas H. Cormen"), [Charles E. Leiserson](/wiki/Charles_E._Leiserson "Charles E. Leiserson") and [Clifford Stein](/wiki/Clifford_Stein "Clifford Stein"). First published in 1990, it has extended into four editions, the latest in 2022.[[A7]](#CITEREFA7)

*Eucalyptus regnans* occurs across a 700 km by 500 km region in the southern Australian states of Victoria and Tasmania. The species grows mostly in cool, mountainous areas that receive [rainfall](/wiki/Rainfall "Rainfall") over 1,000 millimetres (39 in) per year. *E. regnans* reaches its highest elevations of about 1,100 metres (3,600 ft) ASL on the [Errinundra Plateau](/wiki/Errinundra_Plateau "Errinundra Plateau") in north-eastern Victoria, and its lowest elevations near sea-level in some southern parts of its Tasmanian distribution.[[17]](#cite_note-:1-17)

In Victoria, stands of tall trees are found in the [Otway](/wiki/Otway_Ranges "Otway Ranges"), [Dandenong](/wiki/Dandenong_Ranges "Dandenong Ranges"), [Yarra](/wiki/Yarra_Ranges "Yarra Ranges") and [Strzelecki](/wiki/Strzelecki_Ranges "Strzelecki Ranges") ranges as well as [Mount Disappointment](/wiki/Mount_Disappointment_(Australia) "Mount Disappointment (Australia)") and [East Gippsland](/wiki/East_Gippsland "East Gippsland").[[23]](#cite_note-Mifsud2002-23) However, the distribution is much reduced. Most of the *E. regnans* forest across Gippsland was cleared for farmland between 1860 and 1880, and in the Otway Ranges between 1880 and 1900, while severe bushfires hit in 1851, 1898 and 1939.[[15]](#cite_note-Ashton_1953-15) In Tasmania, *E. regnans* is found in the [Huon](/wiki/Huon_Valley "Huon Valley") and [Derwent River](/wiki/River_Derwent_(Tasmania) "River Derwent (Tasmania)") valleys in the southeast of the state.[[8]](#cite_note-Boland-8)

Jupiter :: Orbital motion and observation :: chunk_0015
Jupiter is the only planet whose [barycentre](/wiki/Barycentre "Barycentre") with the Sun lies outside the volume of the Sun, though by 7% of the Sun's radius.[[133]](#cite_note-139)[[134]](#cite_note-Jupiter-COM-20160730-140) The average distance between Jupiter and the Sun is 778 million km (5.20 AU) and it completes an orbit every 11.86 years. This is approximately two-fifths the orbital period of Saturn, forming a near [orbital resonance](/wiki/Orbital_resonance "Orbital resonance").[[135]](#cite_note-141) The [orbital plane](/wiki/Orbital_plane "Orbital plane") of Jupiter is [inclined](/wiki/Orbital_inclination "Orbital inclination") 1.30° compared to Earth. Because the [eccentricity](/wiki/Orbital_eccentricity "Orbital eccentricity") of its orbit is 0.049, Jupiter is slightly over 75 million km nearer the Sun at [perihelion](/wiki/Perihelion "Perihelion") than [aphelion](/wiki/Aphelion "Aphelion"),[[3]](#cite_note-fact-5) which means that its orbit is nearly circular. This low eccentricity is at odds with [exoplanet](/wiki/Exoplanet "Exoplanet") discoveries, which have revealed Jupiter-sized planets with very high eccentricities. Models suggest this may be due to there being two giant planets in the Solar System, as the presence of a third or more giant planets tends to induce larger eccentricities.[[136]](#cite_note-142)
